summaries.summary: Chemistry is one of the natural sciences, concerned with the substances that make up matter and the changes they undergo. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as "the science of the properties, composition, and structure of substances (defined as elements and compounds), the transformations they undergo, and the energy that is released or absorbed during these processes," noting that chemistry "is concerned with the properties of atoms and the laws governing their combinations." As a top-level field it serves as an umbrella over numerous specialized subfields, including analytical, inorganic, organic, and physical chemistry, as well as crystallography and electrochemistry, each addressing a distinct aspect of the composition, structure, reactivity, or measurement of chemical systems. Its central focus on atoms, molecules, and their transformations distinguishes it from neighboring natural-science fields while linking it closely to physics, the earth sciences, and the life sciences.

summaries.summary: Astronomy is the natural science devoted to celestial objects and the phenomena that occur beyond Earth's atmosphere. The Encyclopaedia Britannica characterizes it as the "science that encompasses the study of all extraterrestrial objects and phenomena," adding that "since the late 19th century, astronomy has expanded to include astrophysics, the application of physical and chemical knowledge to an understanding of the nature of celestial objects." As a top-level field within the natural sciences, it studies bodies such as stars, planets, galaxies, and the interstellar and intergalactic medium, as well as the structure and evolution of the universe as a whole. Modern astronomy draws heavily on physics and chemistry through astrophysics, and on observational techniques spanning the electromagnetic spectrum and beyond. It is conventionally treated as a discipline distinct from, though closely allied with, physics and the other physical sciences.

summaries.summary: The earth sciences form the top-level natural-science field concerned with the planet Earth as a physical system. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines them as "the fields of study concerned with the solid Earth, its waters, and the air that envelops it," noting that "included are the geologic, hydrologic, and atmospheric sciences" and that "their broad aim is to understand Earth's present features and past evolution and to use this knowledge to benefit humankind." As an umbrella field, the earth sciences encompass a range of specialized disciplines—among them geology, which studies the solid Earth, alongside the sciences of the oceans, fresh waters, and atmosphere. The field investigates Earth's composition, structure, processes, and history across spatial and temporal scales, and it connects closely with the other natural sciences, including chemistry and physics, through the study of materials, energy, and planetary processes.

summaries.summary: Analytical chemistry is the subfield of chemistry concerned with determining the composition of matter and the identity, quantity, and structure of its components. The Encyclopaedia Britannica, treating the subject under chemical analysis, describes it as the "determination of the physical properties or chemical composition of samples of matter," noting that "a large body of systematic procedures intended for these purposes has been continuously evolving in close association with the development of other branches of the physical sciences." The disciplinary community frames the field around measurement science: the journal Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry states that its scope covers "fundamental and applied topics of analytical and bioanalytical measurement science" and "ranges from novel measurement platforms and their characterization to multidisciplinary approaches." The subfield develops and applies methods of qualitative and quantitative analysis, instrumentation, and separation and detection techniques used throughout the natural sciences.

summaries.summary: Inorganic chemistry is the subfield of chemistry concerned with the elements and compounds that fall outside the domain of carbon-based organic chemistry. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "field of science concerned with the composition, properties, and structure of chemical elements and compounds that contain little or no carbon," and explicitly contrasts it with organic chemistry: "It is distinguished from organic chemistry, which studies compounds that contain carbon atoms." The subfield encompasses the chemistry of metals and minerals, coordination compounds, main-group and transition-element species, and solid-state and organometallic systems, addressing their synthesis, bonding, structure, and reactivity. Within the broader field of chemistry it occupies a recognized major subdivision alongside the organic, physical, and analytical subfields, and it underpins areas such as materials science, catalysis, and the study of inorganic substances throughout the natural sciences.

summaries.summary: Organic chemistry is the subfield of chemistry devoted to compounds of carbon. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "field of science concerned with the composition, properties, and structure of chemical elements and compounds that contain carbon atoms," and explains the field's breadth by noting that "carbon is unique in the variety and extent of structures that can result from the three-dimensional connections of its atoms." The subfield studies the structure, properties, synthesis, and reactions of carbon-containing molecules, ranging from small hydrocarbons to large and structurally elaborate compounds. Within the broader field of chemistry it constitutes a recognized major subdivision, distinguished from inorganic chemistry by its focus on carbon, and it connects closely with the life sciences and with applied areas that rely on the synthesis and transformation of carbon compounds.

summaries.summary: Physical chemistry is the subfield of chemistry that applies the principles of physics to chemical systems. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as the "branch of chemistry concerned with interactions and transformations of materials," explaining that, "unlike other branches, it deals with the principles of physics underlying all chemical interactions, seeking to measure, correlate, and explain the quantitative aspects of reactions." The subfield encompasses areas such as thermodynamics, chemical kinetics, quantum chemistry, spectroscopy, electrochemistry, and statistical mechanics, providing the quantitative and theoretical foundations used across the rest of chemistry. Within the broader field it forms a recognized major subdivision alongside the analytical, inorganic, and organic subfields, and it serves as a bridge between chemistry and physics in the study of how matter behaves at the molecular and bulk levels.

summaries.summary: Crystallography is the subfield concerned with the internal arrangement of matter in crystalline solids. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "branch of science that deals with discerning the arrangement and bonding of atoms in crystalline solids and with the geometric structure of crystal lattices," and notes that "classically, the optical properties of crystals were of value in mineralogy and chemistry for the identification of substances." The subfield studies how atoms, ions, and molecules are ordered in periodic structures and the symmetry and geometry of crystal lattices, and it develops and applies experimental methods—diffraction techniques in particular—for determining such structures. Historically allied with mineralogy and chemistry, crystallography provides structural information used widely across the natural sciences, including in the study of minerals, inorganic and organic compounds, and biological macromolecules.

summaries.summary: Electrochemistry is the subfield of chemistry that studies the relationship between electricity and chemical change. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "branch of chemistry concerned with the relation between electricity and chemical change," noting that "many spontaneously occurring chemical reactions liberate electrical energy, and some of these reactions are used in batteries and fuel cells to produce electric power," while conversely electric energy can be used to drive chemical reactions. The subfield encompasses the study of oxidation–reduction processes, electrodes and electrolytes, electrolysis, and the behavior of ions and charge transfer at interfaces. It underlies technologies such as batteries, fuel cells, electroplating, and corrosion science, and is conventionally treated as closely associated with physical chemistry within the broader field of chemistry.

summaries.summary: Quantum information science is an emerging field at the intersection of quantum physics and information theory. NIST describes it as a field that "marries two of the 20th century's most important scientific developments: quantum physics and information theory," and characterizes it as "using the smallest bits of matter and energy — electrons inside an atom, tiny circuits, massless particles of light — to store, carry and process information." The field is broader than quantum computing alone: NIST notes that while "scientists around the world are developing quantum computers," "other focus areas of quantum information science include quantum sensors for ultra-high-precision measurements and quantum networks that could link devices across cities, nations and ultimately the globe." The physics community recognizes it as a top-level research discipline; the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) taxonomy lists "Quantum Information, Science & Technology" as a discipline-level research area, spanning quantum computation, communication, sensing, and related foundations.
